newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien defends Quebec roots.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien defends Quebec roots.

text.p: Seeking to boost his low popularity in his native Quebec, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien on Thursday defended his French-speaking roots as he campaigned in the province for the June 2 federal election.
In a speech in the 389-year-old capital of this province of 7.1 million people, Chretien said he was disgusted by Conservative leader Jean Charest's attempt to question his Quebec heritage.

"It is completely unacceptable. He should be ashamed and his party should be ashamed," Chretien told a partisan crowd of more than 1,000 people. "I am proud to be a Quebecker and proud to be Canadian."

Chretien, leader of the ruling Liberals, was referring to an article on Thursday in Le Journal de Montreal in which Charest was quoted as saying that Chretien's fiscal austerity policies made him "a guy from Ottawa."
"Mr. Chretien seems not to come from Quebec and that is reflected in his choices," Charest told the newspaper.
It was the second time in the campaign that Charest, also a Quebecker, questioned Chretien's loyalty to Quebec.
Polls show that Charest is the most popular federal party leader in Quebec, with Chretien a distant third after separatist Bloc Quebecois leader Gilles Duceppe.
Chretien also faces a tough fight against the local Bloc Quebecois candidate to retain the House of Commons seat for his hometown electoral district.

By contrast, Chretien has been one of the most popular prime ministers in decades in English Canada. The Liberals won the 1993 national election with a strong majority, but the Bloc Quebecois won 54 of Quebec's 75 seats vs. 19 for the Liberals.

In his speech, Chretien spoke of growing up in Shawinigan, Quebec -- an industrial city halfway between Montreal and Quebec City -- and his years as a graduate student at Laval University in Quebec City.
Chretien focused on economic issues, but said one of his main priorities was to reinforce national unity.
